how: Study, not a backtest. The heatmap page FAQ, Walls and Wall events tabs, and the footprint, CVD, large-order and learn pages were read in Claude in Chrome; a Sonnet reader collected 25 analyst and vendor sources (ANALYST_COMMENTARY.md). Each panel was mapped to our engine and a validation recipe written (FIELD_GUIDE.md section 5). Nothing here is evidence of an edge.
window: one evening, 2026-11-01, Binance BTCUSDT perp; wall events cover the loaded 1-minute history (about 2 days)

verdict.label: Walls are events, not levels: in the loaded two days 191 walls were placed, 1 filled, 176 pulled (CoinGlass counter, SEEN). The page is for validation and context; the one new measurable is a wall pulled before touch, which no public source quantifies. Depth-band check on our snapshot filed as a card.

why: CoinGlass FAQ: 'A pulled wall is often more dangerous than a filled one'; 'the biggest walls are the easiest bait'; 'Can I trade straight from the heatmap? Better not.'
Same level placed and pulled five times in ninety minutes on the bid side (1.4 % below) and three times on the ask side (1.0 % above): the FAQ's own spoof signature, live.
Book was ask-heavy by a fifth inside 1 % (-20.4 %), the only big bid rested 2 % below; the imbalance pane 'only counts resting orders ... read it with the trades'.

Analyst consensus (Bookmap, TheKingfisher, Hyblock, Material Indicators): trade what executes, a wall that gets traded into is real, one that vanishes as price nears is bait; liquidation heatmaps are models.

Our bid/ask ratio asks Binance for 100 levels at tick 0.1, which at 78k spans about 10 USD; the page's 1 % band spans about 780 USD and holds 30-90 BTC per 10 USD row, so the snapshot likely sums one or two rows and calls it 1 % (OURS inference; fapi.binance.com unreachable from JIS-NB, check filed for the feed host).
